title: Beyond Prompting: How Builders Actually Train LLMs
subtitle: LoRA, RAG and the cheap way to teach giant models
intro: Your save got 3,000 stars for 23 notebooks that go beyond prompting. The trick isn't retraining a giant - it's teaching it cheaply.
takeaway: You don't retrain the giant model, you add a tiny adapter and a searchable notebook, then measure if it helped.

sections.heading: Analogy: teaching a master chef your recipe
sections.body:
Imagine a master chef who knows every cuisine. You want your grandma's soup, exactly your way.

You don't send the chef back to cooking school. You give a small recipe card: "add more salt, simmer longer." A LoRA adapter is that card — a tiny add-on you train while the big model, the base LLM like LLaMA or Mistral, stays frozen.

sections.heading: Why does this exist? Making giants affordable
sections.body:
Training a giant LLM from scratch costs millions.

LoRA fixes that by training only the small card. QLoRA uses quantization — squishing weights from 16-bit to 4-bit with bitsandbytes — so it fits on one cheap GPU.

RAG is different. RAG means Retrieval-Augmented Generation — letting the model look up fresh facts in your notes with LangChain and a Knowledge Graph like Neo4j, instead of memorizing them.

sections.heading: What can go wrong? When the card and cookbook fail
sections.body:
If you train the card too long on too little data, it overfits — it memorizes your examples and forgets general skills.

4-bit squishing can make answers less precise. RAG can pull the wrong document and the model will quote it confidently. RLHF, learning from human preferences, can learn the wrong preference if ratings are messy.

That's why the repo uses MLflow evaluation to test before you trust.

steps.narration: Start with a giant base LLM that already knows language.
Add a tiny LoRA card, squeezed to 4-bit so it fits cheaply.
Give it a RAG cookbook to look up fresh facts instead of memorizing.
Run MLflow checks to see if answers actually improved.

quiz.q: What is a LoRA adapter in plain words?
options: A full retrain of the giant model
A tiny recipe card you train while the big model stays frozen
A database for looking up facts
A way to delete the base model
quiz.why: LoRA freezes the base LLM and only trains a small added layer, which is cheap and fast.

quiz.q: Why use RAG instead of just more fine-tuning?
options: RAG makes the model remember everything forever
RAG lets the model look up fresh, private facts at answer time
quiz.why: RAG pipelines let the model retrieve current info from your own docs instead of baking it into weights.

quiz.q: What breaks or goes wrong if you fine-tune too much and skip evaluation?
options: The model automatically gets faster and more accurate
It overfits, forgets general skills, and you won't notice without MLflow checks
RAG will automatically fix all mistakes
quiz.why: Over-training on small data causes overfitting and forgetting, and without evaluation you ship a worse model.
